summary: Laura Grace Weldon reflects on why people forget most books they read, citing Julie Beck's Atlantic article that people cram more into their brains than they can hold and tend to retain information tied to relevance or context. She argues books still shape readers deeply, supported by studies on brain connectivity, blood flow, empathy and theory of mind, and closes with Billy Collins's poem 'Forgetfulness'.
one_line: An essay arguing that forgotten books still shape readers, using research on reading's effects on the brain and empathy.
key_facts: Laura Grace Weldon says she reads, on average, four or five books a week.
Julie Beck's article in The Atlantic is titled 'Why We Forget Most of the Books We Read.'
Beck cites a 2009 study showing the average American encounters 100,000 words a day.
Weldon says memories from reading relate to relevance: people hang on to information that most impacts them, intrigues them, or that they put to use.
An Emory University study found participants who read only part of a novel showed significant increases in connectivity between left and right brain regions, lasting several days.
Stanford's Natalie Phillips found an overall increase in blood flow during close reading.
Phillips said each reading style creates distinct brain patterns that are 'far more complex than just work and play.'
Regular readers, according to various studies, are much more likely to volunteer, donate to charity, and vote than non-readers.
Research shows people most transported by fiction and most empathetic toward characters are more likely to express empathy in real life.
Fiction readers score higher on theory of mind, the ability to understand other people's thoughts, emotions, and perspectives.
Researcher Keith Oatley writes that fiction can be thought of as a form of consciousness of selves and others passed from author to reader.
Weldon compares absorbing books to babies learning language: they sink in deep and stay whether or not we can recall them.
Weldon remembers reading The Color Purple while nursing her firstborn and The Kitchen House by Kathleen Grissom so immersed she missed her flight.
The essay closes with Billy Collins's poem 'Forgetfulness', which describes memories retiring to 'the southern hemisphere of the brain.'
Weldon's essay was posted April 16, 2021 on her blog, and it begins with a quotation from Jenny Davidson comparing a library to a city and books to houses.
